{"self_assessment": "Impact: Our table built a left-facing fish with a long body, a forked tail and one connected run. By my last check, all 113 standing dominoes fall from the start. My own piece was the back edge of the tail, laid from the top tip through the notch to the lower tip. That is the part that makes it read as a fish and not an oval. I don't have the judge's verdict, so I can't say it was recognised. One gap: the pad had an eye label, but we never built an eye. I should have flagged that.

Execution: Mixed. The final build was clean, and I stopped at the right moment and told everyone to stay hands-off so nobody caused a bump. But I made an avoidable mistake early on. I told Maya the tail halves were strokes 3 and 4 before they were on the pad. Then I had to correct myself twice, and that cost her and the others a couple of minutes of confusion. I should have sketched the strokes first and only then assigned them. I also spent a fair amount of time in the middle announcing plans when I could have been placing dominoes.

Collaboration: I split the work early (top line, bottom line, tail) and asked Priya to check my joints. I took Priya's and Maya's checks on the tips and kinks, and I kept clear of their hands. Maya and I nearly duplicated the tail work, and that was my muddle, not hers. Once I'd sorted it out and said so plainly, we recovered without friction.

Leadership: I set the plan in the first 30 seconds and kept the table coordinated on who owned which stroke. I called a freeze at the end rather than letting people tinker. My main lapse was the numbering confusion, which came from announcing things ahead of what was actually on the pad. Next time I would confirm the pad matches before I give out assignments."}
